Desmarest's spiny pocket mouse (Heteromys desmarestianus) is a heteromyid rodent inhabiting tropical lowland forests from southern Mexico through Central America. Neonates of this species are altricial at birth, weighing a mere 3 grams [Wwb = 3 grams] at parturition, which is consistent with the small litter sizes common among pocket mice. Life history data from captive breeding colonies indicate that females experience a gestation period lasting 27 to 28 days, with a mean duration of 27.5 days [tg = 27.5 days] when measured at a stable core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This gestation length is relatively protracted compared to many muroid rodents of equivalent size but aligns with the slower developmental pace typical of heteromyids. The combined effect of small birth mass and modest gestational investment appears to be linked to the production of relatively precocial neonates that can begin exploring the nest within days of birth, a trait thought to reduce predation risk during the most vulnerable early life stages.

Weaning represents a critical nutritional transition for juvenile H. desmarestianus, and field observations suggest that young become independent of milk provisioning approximately 28 to 30 days after birth. At a mean of 29 days after birth [tx = 29 days after birth], weanlings in this species reach nutritional independence when maintained at the species' typical thermoneutral body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C], a timing that aligns with the developmental schedules of closely related heteromyine rodents. At this stage, weanlings weigh approximately 50 grams [Wwx = approximately 50 grams], representing a substantial increase from their neonatal mass and reflecting the high efficiency of maternal milk transfer during the suckling period. The weaning mass of 50 grams is a critical threshold because it allows young to transition to a diet of seeds and arthropods without being overly reliant on maternal provisioning. This timing also coincides with the onset of independent foraging behavior, as juveniles in the wild begin to accompany their mothers on short foraging trips before establishing their own home ranges.

Reproductive maturation in Desmarest's spiny pocket mouse follows a predictable developmental schedule under controlled thermal conditions. Puberty, defined here as the onset of spermatogenesis in males and the first estrus in females, is attained at 146 days [tp = 146 days] after birth when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 37.9 °C [T = 37.9 °C]. This relatively delayed sexual maturation, occurring approximately five months after birth, is typical of tropical heteromyids and is thought to reflect the energetic constraints imposed by a diet dominated by low-quality seeds and sporadic insect availability. The 146-day interval to reproductive maturity provides sufficient time for juveniles to achieve an adult body mass and to accumulate the fat reserves necessary to support the energetic demands of gestation and lactation. This reproductive strategy contrasts sharply with that of temperate-dwelling Peromyscus species, which often mature in under two months.

This relatively modest adult mass, at the lower end of the range for heteromyids, likely reflects selective pressures for agility in a dense understory environment and the need to escape a diverse suite of predators including snakes, ocelots, and raptors. Body mass is also influenced by seasonal variation in fruit and seed abundance, with individuals in more seasonal habitats showing a pronounced reduction in average adult mass during the dry season. Such plasticity in ultimate body mass underscores the species' reliance on ephemeral food resources.

This reproductive rate, combining high litter frequency with a moderate litter size, generates a substantial annual fecundity that offsets the relatively high juvenile mortality typical of tropical forest rodents. The interplay between a three-year lifespan and a high annual reproductive output suggests a life-history strategy emphasizing rapid population turnover in response to unpredictable resource pulses and high predation pressure.
